chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Tiny Hill: heavyweight, shrewd businessman, hillbilly-swing band
summary: Tiny Hill weighed over 300 pounds, told jokes, did his own booking and ran a ten-man band playing hillbilly and 'Angry' songs; Horace added jazz to his standards.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: about that sometime. Tiny Hill.
That was a great guy.
Yeah, he was very -- I played some gigs with him.
Is that right?

Yeah, he used to, every now and then, take a job. While he was here at Fort Luyton, he would book someplace, and he would -- he had a nucleus of Denver musicians that worked for him, although most of the time I was working or writing or something, and so I didn't work steadily, but I'd -- I did a few with him.

Well, as you know, number one, Tiny used to weigh over 300 pounds, you know. He was always heavy. And he was the type of guy that had a great sense of humor, and he was funny, always told jokes, you know, and when he'd laugh, man --
His whole thing just shake, yeah.
(Simultaneous remarks)
-- and shake and whatnot. I tell you what, in -- knowing a lot of bandleaders, he was about the greatest businessman --
That's right. He was sharp.
-- that I ever had the pleasure of being around, man. He was strict -- he was business -- when I say business, he was a good businessman, financially, and,

man, he would pay you right, and he would do a lot of his own bookings, you know, even beside the booking offices, (unintelligible) the, you know, booking offices. He knew a lot of people, and my connection with Tiny was back in Illinois. He used to play a lot of those little, small towns. Boy, they loved that guy. He would get up and sing those --
" : An-gry --"
" Angry Man, " and, you know, those things are hits right now with the people, you know.
: Sure.

And he was far ahead of them. And, man, I used to get up in his hotel room sometimes, and he'd open up his suitcase, and he'd have everything just so immaculate, have his cash there and he had his contracts. He was just a strict businessman, you know, and he had a guy that played tenor with him back there. I hope the guy's still living because he was quite a guy -- named Tod Howard. I don't know remember if you ever met him.
: No.

And he had a great drummer with him, you know. A lot of these names, personnel of that band have left me because, you know, you forget about them, that sort of thing, but he usually carried around ten men, you know, and it was a challenge for me because of the type of music that he played, you know.
: Tenor band.

Yeah. Hillbilly and things like that -- but he was anxious to inject a little swing and have a little versatility in his band, and we became the greatest of friends, and I made some things for him, and I made some arrangements for Tiny on the standards, you know, and he told me, says, 'Jazz them up a little bit, not too much,' one of those things, you know.
